title: Evaluate an expression tree
prompt:
The payload is an arithmetic expression tree. It is either a plain number (a leaf), or an object `{ op, l, r }` where `op` is one of `"+"`, `"-"`, `"*"`, `"/"`, and `l` and `r` are themselves expression trees — a number, or another `{ op, l, r }` node, to any depth.

Write a script that evaluates the tree down to a single number.
starter:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun eval(v) = v match {
  ???
}
---
eval(payload)
hints: Every node in the tree is one of exactly two shapes: a plain number, or an operator with two more trees underneath it. Write one test that distinguishes those two shapes, and make the operator case handle its two sides by asking the same question of them again — not by assuming they are already numbers.

A `match` with `case n is Number` and `case o is Object` gives you the two shapes. Inside the Object case, the two sides (`o.l` and `o.r`) have to be run back through the same evaluation before you apply the operator to them — combining them first and checking their type second is the bug that only shows up once a side is itself a node.

Splitting the work into two functions — one that picks the shape, one that applies the operator once both sides are already numbers — is fine, and they can call each other (`eval` calls a helper for the Object case, and that helper calls `eval` again on `o.l` and `o.r`) with no return-type annotation on either. Keep `-` and `/` in the order the tree gives them: `o.l - o.r`, not the other way around — swapping the order is invisible on `+` and `*` because those don't care, and wrong everywhere else.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun eval(v) = v match {
  case n is Number -> n
  case o is Object -> evalNode(o)
}
fun evalNode(o) = o.op match {
  case "+" -> eval(o.l) + eval(o.r)
  case "-" -> eval(o.l) - eval(o.r)
  case "*" -> eval(o.l) * eval(o.r)
  case "/" -> eval(o.l) / eval(o.r)
}
---
eval(payload)

mustFail.why: handles one level: combines o.l and o.r directly instead of recursing into them first, so it throws the moment either side is itself a node rather than a number
swaps the operand order (r - l instead of l - r, r / l instead of l / r) — invisible on + and *, wrong on every - and / node

explanation.approach: The tree has exactly two shapes at every level: a plain number, or a node with an operator and two more trees underneath it. `match` picks the shape with `case n is Number` and `case o is Object`. The number case is the leaf — it just returns itself. The object case cannot apply its operator to `o.l` and `o.r` directly, because those are trees too, not necessarily numbers; they have to go through `eval` again first. Splitting that into two functions — `eval` for the shape test, `evalNode` for applying the operator once both sides are already evaluated — makes them mutually recursive (`eval` calls `evalNode`, `evalNode` calls `eval`), and neither needs a return-type annotation to compile. The near-miss is applying the operator before recursing: it happens to work when both sides are already numbers, and throws the instant one of them is not.

snippets.label: The near-miss: applying the operator before recursing
snippets.note: `o.l` is itself a node, not a number, and `+` cannot be applied between an Object and a Number. This version never calls `eval` again on `o.l` or `o.r` — it just applies the operator to whatever is there.

snippets.label: The same near-miss, on a tree that happens to be only one level deep
snippets.note: This is why the bug ships: on a flat tree `o.l` and `o.r` already are numbers, so skipping the recursive call is invisible until a deeper tree arrives.

snippets.note: `10 - 4` is `6`; this version computes `4 - 10`. The sample tree's root is `+` and its nested node is `*`, both commutative, so this exact bug would pass the sample case and only shows up on a `-` or `/` node.
